question.text: How does the 'smile' shape of the volatility curve differ between equity and currency options?

answer.text: Equity options typically show a negative skew (smirk) with higher IV for OTM puts; currency options tend to show a more symmetric smile or slight skew depending on the market's directional expectations for the currency
Both equity and currency options always show identical smile shapes
Only equity options have a volatility smile; currency options have flat IV across strikes
Equity options show a symmetric smile; currency options show a steep skew

explanation.text: The Logic: In equity option markets, the predominant pattern is a negative skew (smirk): implied volatility is higher for lower-strike (OTM put) options because investors persistently demand downside protection against sharp market falls. In currency option markets, by contrast, the two currencies in a pair can each move up or down, so demand for OTM call protection and OTM put protection is more balanced and the resulting IV curve is typically a more symmetric "smile" — though directional expectations (captured in the risk-reversal premium) can tilt it either way. The Trap: "Always identical" ignores the structural difference between asset classes. "Only equity options have a smile" is incorrect — currency options also exhibit a smile, just usually more symmetric. The "equity symmetric / currency steep skew" option reverses the typical pattern. Note: The cited NISM workbooks (Series I, IV, VIII pages checked) cover implied volatility and vega but do not, on the pages checked, present a comparison of equity negative skew versus currency smile. The framing above is general derivatives-market knowledge.
